passage:
Aunt Shalini pressed a small parcel into Lalremsiami's hands ten minutes before the bus to Aizawl left. “Open it, quick, I want to see!” Inside were woollen socks, bright green and stiff as cardboard. Lalremsiami's nose twitched and her mouth began to twist. She pressed her lips into a smile. “Thank you, Aunty. They look warm.” Shalini beamed, hugged her and ran for the bus.
Her father, who had seen, said quietly, “That was kind. You can always tell me if you don't like something.”
Lalremsiami shrugged. “I hate the colour. But she tried so hard.”

qa.q: What did Shalini give Lalremsiami?
qa.a: She gave her a parcel with woollen socks, bright green and stiff as cardboard.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she pressed her lips into a smile, and what else could be going on?
qa.a: She disliked the socks but did not want to hurt her aunt, so she hid the grimace. She may also have felt touched that her aunt tried, and rushed because the bus was about to leave.

qa.q: What could her father do next?
qa.a: Keep the door open, as he did, so she can say what she really thinks in private, and gently notice if she often hides real upset.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel seeing the smile?
qa.a: Happy and hurried, believing the gift landed well. If she had seen the grimace she would probably have felt hurt.

grounding: A child swallows a grimace at an unwanted gift to spare someone's feelings; a trusted adult leaves room for honesty.

passage:
At Uma Aunty's flat in Pune, Pankaj took a bite of the bitter gourd curry she had cooked specially for the guests. It was so bitter his eyes watered, and for a second his mouth pulled sideways. He smoothed his face. “Mmm, nice, Aunty.” She smiled and put another spoonful on his plate.
In the lift afterwards his shoulders dropped. “It was so bitter,” he whispered to his mother.
“You were polite,” she said. “You can always tell me the truth at home.”

qa.q: What did Uma Aunty cook for the guests?
qa.a: She cooked bitter gourd curry.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he said “Mmm, nice, Aunty”?
qa.a: He found the curry very bitter but did not want to hurt Uma Aunty, so he smoothed his face. He may also have wanted to be a good guest for his mother's sake.

qa.q: How could his mother respond in the lift, and what should she watch for?
qa.a: She can thank him for being polite and let him know he can be honest with her, while gently noticing if he often hides real upset.

qa.q: How might Uma Aunty feel when Pankaj says it is nice?
qa.a: Pleased that a guest enjoyed her cooking. She has no idea he found it bitter, which shows how well a polite face can work.

grounding: A child masks a grimace at unpleasant food as a display rule; the trusted parent is told the truth.

subtype: Hiding a grimace to be polite [Regulating]
passage: “I made karela specially, Gargi. Your favourite, na?” Nirmala Nani beamed across the table. Gargi took a bite. Her jaw stopped for a second. Then she swallowed and smiled. “Mm. Very… crispy, Nani.” “Take more!” “I'm quite full from school.” On the drive home, Mummy glanced at her. “You hate karela.” “I didn't want Nani to feel bad. She stood in the kitchen for ages.” “That was kind. You don't have to eat things you hate every time, though. You can say, ‘Just a little, Nani.’” Gargi thought about it. “Next time.” “And if something really bothers you, you tell me. Deal?” “Deal.”

qa.q: What did Nirmala Nani make for Gargi?
qa.a: Nirmala Nani made karela.

qa.q: Why did Gargi smile after her jaw stopped?
qa.a: She disliked the karela but felt affection for Nani and didn't want to hurt her after all that cooking, so she hid the grimace.

qa.q: What middle way did Mummy offer Gargi?
qa.a: She suggested asking for just a little, and reminded Gargi to tell her if something really bothers her.

qa.q: How might Nani feel if she ever learned Gargi hates karela?
qa.a: She might feel a bit embarrassed but also touched that Gargi protected her feelings.

grounding: Shows a child swallowing a grimace at disliked food to spare a grandparent's feelings, and a parent keeping the door open for real worries.

subtype: Hiding a grimace to be polite [Regulating]
passage: I'm Yash, and last month Ayesha from my class gave me a birthday present she had knitted herself: a bright orange cap, very scratchy. When I pulled it on, my forehead itched like mad. I felt my face start to scrunch, so I pushed my mouth into a smile and said, “Wow, you made this?” Ayesha said it took her three weeks. I wore it for the whole party, even though my ears burned. That night I told my dad the truth, and he laughed and said it was a kind sort of pretending. Now I wear it over a softer cap on cold mornings.

qa.q: How long did Ayesha say the cap took her?
qa.a: Ayesha said it took her three weeks.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when the cap first went on?
qa.a: Yash felt itchy and uncomfortable but also grateful and worried about hurting Ayesha, so the grimace turned into a smile.

qa.q: Why was telling Dad the truth later a wise step?
qa.a: It let Yash be honest with a trusted adult while still protecting Ayesha's feelings, so the polite face didn't hide anything that mattered.

qa.q: What would Ayesha have felt if Yash had grimaced openly?
qa.a: Ayesha might have felt hurt and embarrassed after three weeks of knitting.

grounding: Shows a child hiding a grimace at an unwanted gift to avoid hurting the giver, while staying honest with a trusted adult.

subtype: Hiding a grimace to be polite [Regulating]
passage: Class 4 notebook, Friday. Vandana, class teacher. Uday is the most polite child I teach. When the school lunch was burnt dal today, he smiled and said, “It's good, ma'am.” That's a fine social skill. But this week he also smiled after falling hard on the steps, knee bleeding, and after Rehan took his seat again. His jaw was tight each time. I don't want to break his manners; I want him to know he can drop them with me. At home time I sat with him and said, “You don't have to look fine with me. What's been hard this week?” He was quiet, then told me about the seat. I spoke to Rehan's group before the buses left.

qa.q: What did Uday say about the burnt dal?
qa.a: Uday smiled and said, “It's good, ma'am.”

qa.q: What might Uday's tight jaw behind the smiles suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was hurt or upset underneath, hiding pain and frustration behind politeness; he may also simply have been trying hard to be good.

qa.q: How did Vandana respect Uday's manners while checking on him?
qa.a: She valued his politeness but sat with him privately, told him he didn't have to look fine with her and asked what had been hard.

qa.q: How might Uday see school differently after Vandana's question?
qa.a: He might feel safer, knowing at least one adult notices when a smile covers something and will act on it the same day.

grounding: Shows a child's polite hiding of a grimace as a social skill, and a teacher gently noticing when it also hides real distress.

subtype: Hiding a grimace to be polite [Regulating]
passage:
Saturday

Dear Diary,
Saurabh Chacha came from Nagpur and brought me a jumper he knitted himself. It is mustard yellow with a green frog on it, and it is SO scratchy. When I opened it, my face wanted to go "eww". I pressed my lips together and said, "Thank you, Chacha, the frog is so cute!" He looked so pleased he did a little clap. At dinner Chachi's karela sabzi was really bitter, and I did the same trick. Tonight I told Mummy both real faces. She laughed and said I can always show her the real face, even when I'm polite outside.

Sharmila

qa.q: What colour was the jumper Saurabh Chacha knitted?
qa.a: Mustard yellow with a green frog on it.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila press lips together and praise the frog?
qa.a: Sharmila disliked the scratchy jumper and felt disappointed, but didn't want to hurt Chacha, who had knitted it by hand.

qa.q: How did Mummy handle Sharmila's "real faces"?
qa.a: Mummy laughed and said the real face can always be shown at home, so being polite outside doesn't mean hiding feelings from trusted people.

qa.q: How does Saurabh Chacha experience the thank-you?
qa.a: He looks so pleased he claps, so he feels his handmade gift is loved; he never sees the scratchy-jumper face.

grounding: It is a child's diary about swallowing a grimace at an unwanted gift and bitter food to spare feelings, while still sharing the real reaction with a trusted adult.
